name: Spaghetti
alt: A close-up photo of a bundle of long, thin, round noodles lying together.
facts: A single strand is long enough that twirling it around a fork takes most kids a few tries to master.
It used to be sold by the yard before factories started packaging it by weight in boxes.
Snapping a handful in half before cooking is considered a kitchen crime in much of Italy.

name: Penne
alt: A close-up photo of short, ridged tube-shaped noodles with diagonally cut ends.
facts: Its angled ends are cut to look like the tip of a quill pen.
The ridges on its outside aren't just decoration — they help sauce cling on instead of sliding off.
Its hollow tube shape means a little pocket of sauce can hide inside every single piece.

name: Fusilli
alt: A close-up photo of corkscrew-shaped noodles twisted into tight spirals.
facts: Its spiral shape was traditionally made by winding fresh dough around a thin knitting needle.
Because it's curly instead of smooth, every twist traps tiny bits of sauce.
It's a popular pick for cold pasta salads since the twists hold dressing well even after cooling.

name: Rigatoni
alt: A close-up photo of large, ridged tube-shaped noodles with straight-cut ends.
facts: It's one of the bigger tube shapes, wide enough that cheese or meat can be stuffed inside.
Its ridged surface comes from the grooved metal dies the dough gets pushed through.
Its wide tube and straight ends make it a favorite for hearty baked casseroles.

name: Farfalle
alt: A close-up photo of bowtie-shaped noodles with pinched, ruffled centers.
facts: Its name means 'butterflies' in Italian, after its pinched, winged shape.
Home cooks once pinched the centers of little dough rectangles by hand to make this shape.
Its ruffled edges and pinched waist make it easy to spot in any pasta salad.

name: Linguine
alt: A close-up photo of long, flat, narrow ribbon-shaped noodles.
facts: Its name comes from the Italian word for 'little tongues,' describing its flat, narrow shape.
It's flatter than a round strand noodle but much narrower than a wide ribbon noodle.
It pairs well with seafood sauces because its flatter shape catches small bits of clam or shrimp.

name: Fettuccine
alt: A close-up photo of long, flat, wide ribbon-shaped noodles.
facts: Its name means 'little ribbons' in Italian, describing its broad, flat shape.
It's traditionally cut from a sheet of fresh egg dough rolled out and sliced into wide strips.
Its wide surface area makes it especially good at holding onto thick, creamy sauces.

name: Lasagna
alt: A close-up photo of wide, flat rectangular pasta sheets fanned out on a table.
facts: It's rolled out wide and flat, then layered with sauce and cheese in between each sheet.
Some versions have ruffled edges on both sides, which helps each layer grip the one above it.
A single sheet is big enough to cover almost an entire baking dish on its own.

name: Ravioli
alt: A close-up photo of square pasta pockets with crimped edges, arranged in neat rows on a tray.
facts: Each little square is really two layers of dough pressed together around a hidden filling.
Its crimped, wavy edges aren't just for looks — they help seal in whatever filling is tucked inside.
Long ago, cooks sealed the edges by hand with just their fingers before crimping tools existed.

name: Tortellini
alt: A close-up photo of small ring-shaped stuffed pasta scattered on a wooden surface.
facts: Legend says its curled ring shape was inspired by a cook peeking at a belly button through a keyhole.
It's folded around a filling, then pinched into a tiny ring instead of staying a flat square.
It's small enough to eat by the spoonful, often served floating in a warm broth.

name: Orzo
alt: A close-up photo of small grain-shaped noodles scattered next to a coin for scale.
facts: Its name means 'barley' in Italian, since it was shaped to look like a plump grain.
It's small enough to scoop up with a spoon instead of twirling on a fork.
It cooks much faster than larger pasta shapes because each piece is so tiny.

name: Macaroni
alt: A close-up photo of two small curved tube-shaped noodles crossed over each other.
facts: Its short, curved tube is hollow all the way through, perfect for trapping melted cheese.
It became famous in America mostly thanks to a cheesy baked dish named after it.
Its gentle curve happens naturally as the short tube dries and slightly bends.

name: Ziti
alt: A close-up photo of medium, smooth, straight tube-shaped noodles bundled together.
facts: Unlike some of its ridged cousins, its outer surface is smooth instead of grooved.
It's traditionally served at celebrations in parts of Italy, especially weddings.
Its straight hollow tube is wide enough that sauce can seep all the way inside.

name: Conchiglie
alt: A close-up photo of shell-shaped noodles with ridged outer curves.
facts: Its name means 'shells' in Italian, after its curved, seashell-like shape.
Its hollow, cupped shape is great at scooping up chunky sauce like a tiny spoon.
Bigger versions of this same shape are often stuffed with cheese and baked.

name: Cavatappi
alt: A close-up photo of small corkscrew-shaped hollow tube noodles scattered together.
facts: Its name means 'corkscrew' in Italian, describing its spiral tube shape.
It's basically a hollow tube that's been twisted into a spiral instead of left straight.
Its ridged, curly shape makes it a favorite for cold pasta salads at picnics.
